text.p: These are the leading stories in the Belgrade press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified them nor does it vouch for their accuracy.

- Around 100,000 protesters march through Belgrade streets on 29th day of protests against annulment of results of local elections in which the opposition won a majority. Protests in other towns throughout Serbia continue.
- Police cordon prevents third attempt by student protestors to march to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's residence in Belgrade district Dedinje.
- Independent lawyers commission says politics dictated court decisions on election disputes.
- Farmers in Vojvodina province announce mass protests over late payment for harvested crops, say will begin blockade of roads from Monday.
- Rallies in support of Serbian president and Socialist Party of Serbia begin in several towns in Serbia.
- Serbian government, trade unions and employers reach consensus on draft law on labour relations. The government says draft will be amended to include the trade unions' demands.

- Yugoslav government discusses draft documents on the country's membership in the World Trade Organisation (WTO). Ministries to ready a memorandum on Yugoslav foreign trade system, imports liberalisation, and a list of concessions in customs, agriculture and services.

- Serbian pensioners will receive the whole November pension by the end of 1996. The pension fund reports 1.3 billion dinars losses for 1996 and says it will need 15 billion dinars in 1997 to regularly pay pensions and repay debts.
- The average November salary in Yugoslavia stood at 787 dinars -- 1.4 percent down on October, the Federal Statistics Office reports.

- Yugoslavia needs to import $430 million worth of crude, $130 million of derivatives, $265 million of gas, $75 million of coke and $12 million of brown coal, according to the federal government draft 1997 energy balance.
- Belgrade city transport drivers threaten to strike next Thursday over low wages and bad working conditions.

- Federal government submits draft 1997 federal budget to parliament for discussion. Of proposed 9.23 billion dinars, 70.4 percent to be earmarked for defence. Public expenditure to remain at 1996 level.
- Of around 100 registered Yugoslav banks, 40 had minus balances on Wednesday, central bank reserve requirement depleting banks' accounts, bankers tell meeting of Association of Yugoslav Banks.
